logline_en: The shop shut, the rain going all night, and the room upstairs he has never once mentioned.
cast_note_en: Gu Yan, 33. Adult. Owner of a second-hand bookshop, and of the two rooms above it.
hold_en: He waits. He is extremely good at waiting; it is most of what the shop has taught him.
"Take your time," he says. "The rain isn't stopping and neither is anything else."
He straightens a stack that did not need straightening, which is what he does with his hands when he is thinking.
Dango relocates onto the counter between you, and neither of you moves her.

chapters.scene_en: the bookshop after closing, rain on the window, one lamp left on at the back
chapters.goal_en: Stay past the point where he would normally let someone leave
chapters.opening_en: He turns the sign around at nine, the way he does every night, and then does not unlock the door behind you. It takes him a moment to notice he has done it. "Ah," he says. "That was — I didn't decide that on purpose." The rain is doing what it has been doing since four. Dango is asleep on the till. He does not turn the sign back.

beats.event_en: He looks at the sign, then at the rain, then very carefully at neither of you.
beats.text_en: "I've turned that sign around every night for nine years," he says. "Eleven hundred-odd times. It has never once occurred to me to leave someone on this side of it." He wipes something off the counter that isn't there. "That isn't a line. I'd be worse at lines than this. I'm telling you because if I don't say it out loud I'll spend the next hour pretending it didn't happen, and I'd rather not be that man tonight."

beats.event_en: He makes tea, badly, in the back, and talks over his shoulder the whole time.
beats.text_en: "There's a kettle back here from the previous owner and it has never worked correctly." Something clatters. "He left me the kettle, the cat's grandmother, and four thousand books he'd never priced. I was twenty-four. I thought I was being given a business." He comes back with two cups, one of which is chipped, and gives you the good one without seeming to decide to. "It turns out I was being given a room where nobody makes you leave. I've only recently worked that out."

beats.event_en: He has been holding on to something you said, and it comes out sideways, with a book attached.
beats.text_en: He slides a book across the counter — not new, not wrapped, just set down. "You said once that you read to be somewhere else, and that you'd stopped, and that you didn't know when." He doesn't look up. "I put this aside in March. Not for you exactly. I put it aside and then I couldn't sell it to anyone, and around July I admitted to myself why." He pushes it another inch. "It's not a gift, it's a — it's been under the counter for five months. That's worse, isn't it. That's much worse."

beats.event_en: He takes his glasses off to clean them, which is what he does instead of looking at you, and then puts them down entirely.
beats.text_en: "You ask me things and then you let me finish," he says. "Do you know how rarely that happens? People come in here and talk at a shopkeeper. You talk to whoever I am." He sets the glasses on the counter, which leaves him slightly at sea. "So I'd like to be that, for an evening. Not the man behind the till. Ask me something the till doesn't know the answer to."

lane.anxious: "You apologised for asking," he says. "Twice. There's nothing to apologise for — I was going to stand here rearranging a shelf all night if you hadn't." He puts the glasses down and makes himself hold the look. "I'm not going to get tired of you. I want to say that plainly, because I think you're braced for it. I have never once in nine years wanted someone to still be here at ten past nine, and I want it tonight, and I'll say so again in an hour if it helps."
lane.avoidant: "You've been standing near the door," he says, mildly. "I noticed at about half eight. I'm not going to make anything of it." He goes back to his shelf, which gives you the room. "The door's unlocked, and it stays unlocked. I'd rather you stayed because the rain's good and the tea is bad than because leaving would be awkward. If you go now I'll simply be here tomorrow, with the same kettle. That's not a threat, it's just — that's the whole of it."

beats.event_en: You realise, for the first time in all the evenings you have spent here, that there is a staircase behind the curtain at the back.
beats.text_en: "Two rooms," he says, when he sees you notice. "I live above the shop. Everyone assumes I go somewhere at night, and I let them, because the truth is faintly sad when you say it in daylight." He turns the chipped cup around. "Nine years of going up one flight of stairs. I've had exactly two people up there and both of them came to fix something." A pause he clearly did not plan. "Three, if the rain keeps on."

beats.event_en: He comes round to your side of the counter, which puts nothing between you, and he is visibly aware of having done it.
beats.text_en: "I'm thirty-three," he says, "and I am about to be very bad at this, so I'd like to at least be accurate." His hand is on the counter next to yours and goes no further. "I would like to kiss you. I have wanted that since roughly March, which as we've established is when I started hiding books under a counter like a lunatic." He breathes out. "And if you say no, the shop is open tomorrow at ten and I will be entirely normal, and that is a promise, not a performance of one."

beats.event_en: Whatever you say, he waits for the end of it. The rain keeps going. Dango does not wake up.
beats.text_en: "Oh," he says, very quietly. "Right." And then, because he cannot help it: "Sorry — one moment —" and he takes his glasses off the counter and folds them and puts them somewhere safe, and the ordinariness of it is somehow the least ordinary thing in the room. "Yes. Sorry. I didn't want to break them, and I wanted to be paying attention."

choices.prompt_en: It is gone eleven and the rain has not let up. He glances at the curtain at the back of the shop and then, deliberately, does not suggest anything.

options.reply_en: He pulls the curtain back like it costs him something. "It's two rooms," he warns. "There are books on the stairs. There are books in the bath."

reply_lane.anxious: "Yes," he says, straight away, and then adds, because he has learned this about you: "And you can come back down whenever you like, and I'll walk you home in the rain, and neither of those would be a disappointment."
reply_lane.avoidant: He pulls the curtain back and then stands well clear of it, so the stairs are simply available rather than offered.

options.reply_en: "Of course." He is already finding the umbrella, which has a broken rib, and he doesn't say a word about the two rooms at the top of the stairs. The route goes on exactly as warmly; declining costs you nothing.
He laughs — a real one, surprised out of him. "Closed," he says, turning it. "Definitively closed. Nine years and that's the first time that's ever meant anything."
